title: Prior summer heat peaks gave no clear common link to next-year butterfly indices in England, Scotland and Wales in 1981-2024
abstract: We tested whether a short summer heat peak was linked to a lower butterfly index in the next year, beyond seasonal mean temperature and rain. We used a fixed set of nine species in England, Scotland and Wales in retained 1981-2024 records. A fixed weather-grid mask removed changes in coastal coverage. Four outcome years per country failed daily weather coverage, leaving 40 annual outcomes. The heat measure was the highest three-day mean daily maximum temperature minus its summer mean. Full-record slopes were +0.0123, -0.0127 and +0.0068 log10 index units per C. All three corrected intervals included zero. All six country and period intervals also included zero. Coverage and model-choice checks did not establish a common adverse link. Small early samples, correlated country weather, coarse exposure, selected species, source-index error and unknown detection limit inference. The result does not establish absence of a heat effect or a causal climate-change effect. The package adds daily regional heat data, source-mask audits, exact source hashes, code, all estimates and numerical checks.

display.caption: Prior summer heat-peak slopes. Full-record intervals correct for three tests. Period intervals correct for six tests. All intervals include zero.

citations.reason: Prior seasonal-weather and response-measure test uses the same biological source. We rebuild inputs and add a daily heat-peak measure.
Prior seasonal-weather model-shape test shares the same nine species. Our exposure test differs; this is not independent biological data.
Prior observation-offset restriction for rain motivates a model review. We do not apply its zero-sum restriction to a free lag-index model.
